pride_data.title: Identification of potential self-interaction sites on golgin Imh1-C213 by cross-linking mass spectrometry
pride_data.projectDescription: The golgins are long coiled-coil proteins involved in vesicular transport to the Golgi, a process that contributes to Golgi function and integrity. Previous studies have elucidated that their self-interaction and their interaction with small GTPase Arl1 are critical for their Golgi localization. Here, we report that glycerol regulates Golgi localization of Imh1, a prototypic yeast golgin. Experimentally, we observed that cellular conditions leading to reduced intracellular glycerol levels trigger the release of Imh1 from the Golgi, whereas restoring glycerol levels reverses this effect. Given that glycerol is a well-documented molecular chaperone, we investigated its impact on the conformation of the Imh1 C-terminal fragment (Imh1-C213) in vitro, employing limited proteolysis assays. To further understand glycerol-induced conformational changes, we used isotope-labeled BS3-d0/d4 crosslinkers in combination with LC-MS/MS to map potential self-interaction sites on Imh1-C213. Our findings reveal and quantify several distinct cross-linked peptide pairs within Imh1-C213, in both the presence and absence of glycerol. These observed differences likely correspond to glycerol-induced conformational changes, which provide novel insights into the structural dynamics of golgins and their functional regulation within the Golgi apparatus.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Purified Imh1-C213 was exchanged for cross-linking buffer (10 mM Hepes, pH 8.5, 100 mM NaCl) by passing through a SEC column Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva). Protein was then incubated with or without 0.1 M glycerol in cross-linking buffer at 30 ℃ for 1 h. Cross-linking was carried on by incubating 0.1 mg/ml of Imh1-C213 with 0.1 mM nondeuterated (d0) or deuterated (d4) bis(sulfosuccinimidyl)suberate (BS3) (d0/d4, cat 21590/21595, Thermo) at 25 ℃ for 30 min. The cross-linking step was repeated with label swapping. The cross-linking reaction was finally quenched by 50 mM Tris and incubated at 25 ℃ for 15 min. For protein digestion, the equal amounts of BS3-labeled Imh1-C213 proteins (d0:d4 = 1:1) were dissolved in a solution of 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate and then subjected to reduction with 5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine and alkylation with 10 mM methyl methanethiosulfonate in the dark. Samples were digested with trypsin (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) at an enzyme to protein ratio of 1:25 at 37 ℃ overnight. Desalting was performed using a SOURCE 15RPC reversed-phase microcolumn (Cytiva, Uppsala, Sweden), and the resulting peptide mixture was dried in a SpeedVac concentrator. The dried peptides were then resuspended in a 0.1% formic acid (FA, Sigma, St. Louis, MO) solution for further liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis as previously described (doi: 10.1073/pnas.2207414119) with the following modifications. In brief, the cross-linked peptide mixtures in HPLC buffer (0.1% FA) were loaded into a trap column (Zorbax 300SB-C18 column with dimensions of 5 µm, 300 Å, and 0.3 × 5 mm, Agilent Technologies in Santa Clara, CA, USA) at a flow rate of 0.3 μL/min. The salts were washed with HPLC buffer at a flow rate of 20 L/min for 10 min, and the desalted peptides were then separated on a 10 cm analytical C18 column (ACQUITY UPLC M-Class Peptide BEH C18 Column, 130Å, 1.7 µm, 100 µm X 100 mm, Waters Corp., Milford, MA, USA) using a 150 min linear gradient of 99.9% acetonitrile and 0.1% FA. The LC setup was coupled online to an LTQ-Orbitrap Elite Hybrid MS spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated with Xcalibur 2.2 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The experimental apparatus was operated under conditions of positive ionization mode, with the applied spray voltage set to 1.8 kilovolts. Acquisition of MS1 spectra in an MS range of 400–2000 Da (three fragments: m/z 400-800, m/z 700-1100, m/z 1000-1400) was performed using the Orbitrap mass analyzer. For MS2, a higher-energy collisional dissociation with a normalized collision energy of 30% was set for the fragmentation. The resolution was set to 120000 and 15000 for MS1 and MS2, respectively. The dynamic exclusion was set to 60 sec and the top ten ions with the highest intensity were selected for fragmentation.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: The raw spectral data were uploaded to the pLink3 search engine (version 3.0.16, released on 2025-01-11) to identify and quantify the cross-links (doi:10.1038/s41467-019-11337-z). A FASTA database for the Imh1-C213 sequence was created based on Uniprot. The parameters for the pLink3 search included BS3 and BS3 heavy as cross-linkers, with trypsin as the protease allowing for a maximum of two missed cleavages. Methylthio-cysteine was designated as a fixed modification, while oxidation of methionine was treated as a variable modification. Mass tolerances were set at 10 ppm for MS1 and 20 ppm for MS2 data. A false discovery rate of 1% at the spectrum level was applied (doi: 10.1074/mcp.RA120.002028). Only cross-linked peptide pairs with BS3 linkages at lysine residues were included in the analysis, while cross-links at peptide C-termini were excluded, except for those involving the C-terminus of the Imh1-C213 protein. Annotated b and y ions corresponding to the peptide sequences were generated from the identified cross-links and visualized using pLabel software. To ensure robustness, quantitative analysis was performed using a triplicate label-swap approach. Cross-links considered for quantification were those consistently detected in all six experiments and supported by at least one cross-linked peptide spectrum match with a pLink3 spectrum score greater than 0.85, with spectrum quality confirmed manually.
